## Overview

The Gorowa, also known as Fyomi, are a Cushitic ethnic group and Iraqw community inhabiting the Manyara and Dodoma regions of Tanzania. Their language, Gorowa, belongs to the South Cushitic branch of the Afro-Asiatic family. The number of Gorowa people is difficult to establish because national censuses do not record ethnic affiliation or language; the number of Gorowa speakers is estimated to be 132,748. The Gorowa have been in their present location for approximately 250–300 years, or about 10 generations. Their folk-cultural significance in the available sources lies especially in language, oral documentation, sacred landscapes, indigenous land management, rituals, and social gatherings held in forests and sacred groves.

## Festivals & rituals

Traditional Gorowa belief systems regard the natural world as sacred. Indigenous land-management practices inspired by myth developed around this view. Gorowa rituals and social gatherings often take place in forests and sacred groves carefully preserved for these purposes. Large trees, especially ficus, are protected as dwellings of rain-bringing spirits, and various unsustainable land-use practices were prohibited.

## Oral tradition & literature

Older Gorwaa speakers in rural areas have contributed to a large body of linguistic and cultural material, including songs, traditional stories, and uncommon vocabulary. The sources also mention an archive of language and cultural material from the Gorowa people of Babati. The Gorwaa DoReCo corpus contains audio recordings of narrative texts with transcriptions time-aligned at the phone level, translations, and time-aligned morphological annotations.

## Language & religion

Gorowa is a Cushitic language spoken in Tanzania’s Dodoma and Manyara Regions. It is also known as Fiome, Goroa, Gorwaa, Kimbulu, and Ufiomi. As of 2014, an estimated 79,000 people, approximately 60% of the ethnic population, used the language daily. Younger Gorwaa in urban areas viewed the language as less useful and could be reticent to speak it, while codeswitching with Swahili was described as ubiquitous. Some speakers used the exonym Mbulu and said they spoke Kimbulu, although the source identifies this as the Gorwaa language.

Instances of Gorwaa writing are rare and show a great variety of non-standard spellings. The orthography of Iraqw is commonly used for Gorwaa written communication. Traditional Gorowa belief systems see the natural world as sacred, with rituals, sacred groves, rain-bringing spirits, and myth-inspired land-management practices forming part of the documented spiritual landscape.
